title: The Fortresses of Khaybar
subtitle: The Volcanic Basalt Strongholds and the Opening Battles of the Northern Oasis
summary: Following their morning arrival at Khaybar, the Muslim forces confronted a sophisticated network of basalt fortifications spread across three oasis regions—Al-Natat, Al-Shiqq, and Al-Katibah. Facing formidable stone citadels, disciplined garrisons, and deep perimeter ditches, the believers began the arduous siege of Na'im and the surrounding strongholds under the strategic leadership of the Prophet.

sections.text: The Formidable Topography of the Northern Oasis

Rising out of the jagged volcanic terrain approximately ninety-five miles north of Madinah, the fertile basin of Khaybar represented the most heavily fortified settlement in northern Arabia. Unlike the open palm groves of the southern Hijaz, Khaybar was built across rugged fields of black basalt stone known as the Harrah, where natural elevation and volcanic ridges formed insurmountable defensive barriers. For decades, the oasis had flourished as a prosperous agricultural and mercantile sanctuary, protected by formidable stone citadels engineered to withstand prolonged sieges and equipped with subterranean granaries, reliable freshwater springs, and substantial arsenals.

The strategic importance of Khaybar had escalated dramatically following the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir clan from Madinah in the fourth year of the Hijrah. Leaders such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq had settled within its walls, transforming the northern stronghold into an active center of political and military intrigue. From Khaybar, emissaries had journeyed across the desert to finance, coordinate, and incite the vast confederacy of Arab tribes that laid siege to Madinah during the Battle of the Trench. Even after the withdrawal of the Ahzab, the leadership of Khaybar maintained close military alliances with the powerful nomadic tribes of Ghatafan, posing an ongoing existential threat to the peace and security of the fledgling Muslim commonwealth.
The Three Defensive Sectors of Khaybar

Historical accounts preserved by classical chroniclers divide the fortifications of Khaybar into three distinct geographic clusters, each comprising several independent stone redoubts. The first sector, known as Al-Natat, formed the advance defensive line and contained the strongholds of Na'im, Al-Sa'b ibn Mu'adh, and Qal'at al-Zubayr. The second sector, Al-Shiqq, lay adjacent to Al-Natat and encompassed the fortresses of Ubayy and Al-Bari'. Farther to the north lay the third and most formidable sector, Al-Katibah, which housed the impregnable citadels of Al-Qamus—the ancestral seat of the house of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq—alongside Al-Watih and Al-Sulalim.

Before commencing operations, the Prophet executed a masterful maneuver of military isolation. By advancing swiftly along the western approach and pitching his camp at Al-Raji, he severed the primary communication corridor linking Khaybar to their primary allies, the Ghatafan tribes of Najd. When the Ghatafan marshaled their fighters to reinforce Khaybar, alarming noises and reports reached them regarding the security of their own families and herds left behind, compelling them to abandon the expedition and retreat to their pastures. With external reinforcement decisively neutralized, the defenders of Khaybar were forced to rely entirely upon their internal fortifications and stockpiled provisions.
The Opening Assaults on Fort Na'im

Operations began with the assault against Fort Na'im, the southern bastion guarding the approaches to Al-Natat. From their elevated battlements, the defenders rained iron-tipped arrows, heavy basalt boulders, and burning missiles upon the advancing Muslim detachments. The terrain offered little natural shelter, forcing the believers to construct mobile protective mantlets and engage in sharp skirmishes along the rocky slopes. Under the scorching desert sun, repeated sorties from the fortress gates were met with steadfast resolve, but the thick stone architecture resisted immediate penetration.

During these early engagements, casualties mounted on both sides. It was during an assault on the outskirts of Fort Na'im that Mahmud ibn Maslamah was martyred when a heavy millstone was cast down upon him from the parapets. Despite initial setbacks, the Muslim vanguard systematically pressed the siege, cutting off water conduits and repelling defensive counter-attacks. The campaign demanded exceptional physical endurance and spiritual discipline, as supplies of dates and grain were initially scarce among the believers until the outer redoubts were secured.
Methodological Qualification of Early Siege Reports

In reviewing the historical literature of the Khaybar campaign, academic and scholarly rigor necessitates a clear distinction between verified Hadith reports and detailed narratives preserved in classical Seerah texts. While authentic collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim document the departure from Madinah, the morning encounter with the laborers, the prohibition of domestic donkey flesh, and the bestowal of the banner, the intricate day-by-day progression through individual fortresses is primarily recorded in the Maghazi literature of Ibn Ishaq, Al-Waqidi, and Ibn Sa'd. Classical scholars treat these operational accounts with historical respect while acknowledging that specific casualty figures and individual combat details often carry narrative variance.

The early days at Khaybar demonstrated that the confrontation would not be decided by a single pitched battle, but through relentless perseverance against deeply entrenched positions. The fortress walls stood firm, testing the fortitude of the companions who had sworn the Pledge of the Tree, and setting the stage for a dramatic turning point that would alter the course of the northern campaign.

references.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
references.author: Imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari (d. 256 AH)
references.notes: Details the morning arrival at Khaybar, the surprise of the farmers, and the prohibition of domestic donkey meat during the initial siege.

references.title: Sahih Muslim
references.author: Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 261 AH)
references.notes: Narrates the mobilization, the night journey, and the tactical encampment outside the settlements of Khaybar.

references.title: Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah
references.author: Ibn Hisham (d. 218 AH), based on Ibn Ishaq (d. 151 AH)
references.notes: Classical documentation of the fortress clusters (Al-Natat, Al-Shiqq, Al-Katibah) and the military maneuvers at Al-Raji.
